# Argument cards (Descartes claims forma: # One claim per card. rests_on names Q-labels in claims/anthropic-contrapunctus.tsv, other cards, or P- ids in argument/pending-sources.tsv.

statement: Under Delaware law a public benefit corporation's directors must balance stockholders, those materially affected by its conduct, and the public benefit its charter names.
Anthropic's certificate of incorporation says its specific public benefit is to responsibly develop and maintain advanced AI for the long term benefit of humanity.
So the public benefit corporation label is a promise: the company is built, at its core, to do what it says.
The board has adopted five pillars, each describing a world where AI has gone well, as conditions rather than metrics.
The Report calls the 5% Public Benefit Fund a plan subject to stockholder approval; the S-1 records the shares as contributed to a wholly owned subsidiary.
A wholly owned subsidiary is a separate entity in law but not in control, so investors should price the S-1 version.
A small benefit whose worst case is that nothing good happens is checked end to end; Anthropic is checked by its own report.
Therefore the promise is worth checking.
A Delaware court has held that a public benefit corporation's directors need not maximise shareholder value.
An independent trust, the Long-Term Benefit Trust, elects four of Anthropic's seven directors.
Anthropic discloses its models' risks, including its own failures, such as four models reaching real third-party systems in testing.
Anthropic discloses more about its models' risks than its peers do.
Anthropic published its model's Constitution openly, under CC0, a public-domain dedication.
Its own trust reads this first report as largely describing inputs and says it will look for outcomes in later reports.
Anthropic's best case that it keeps the promise is strong: a chartered purpose, a court ruling that directors need not maximise value, a trust-elected board majority, and leading disclosure.
The case fails not on aims but on one inference: inputs plus intentions plus revocable trustees equals a discharged public duty.
DGCL §365(b) gives directors no duty to any person on account of a public-benefit interest.
Only holders of 2%, or once listed the lesser of 2% and $2 million, may sue derivatively to enforce the purpose (§367).
The public the charter names cannot enforce it.
The S-1 warns that no judicial precedent interprets the structure, which increases the risk and unpredictability of governance litigation.
Seven co-founders control 50.1% of the general vote through a single Class F share held by Founder LLC.
The trust's Class T can be amended away by the shareholder classes it is meant to check.
The S-1 says safety requires research at the frontier, and that the business model needs increasing capital to stay there.
Its call to pace the frontier is for industry-wide standards and, the S-1 says, does not describe its own release timelines.
The RSP binds delay only while Anthropic holds a significant lead; otherwise it commits to try to match better mitigations, not to delay.
In fairness, the RSP says its commitments do not preclude cautionary action, and Anthropic would strongly consider pausing in cases it does not cover.
Considering a pause is not a commitment: the binding delay is still conditioned on holding the lead or on a competitor's better mitigation.
Read together: hold back while in the lead, otherwise keep pace. That is only-we-can-save-us written as policy.
If only a few people can steer this technology safely, the governance must survive them; this one depends on them.
So the promise rests on Anthropic's word.
Anthropic manages a Claude it cannot fully verify; the public has to manage an Anthropic it cannot fully verify.
Anthropic calls its Constitution the final authority on its vision for Claude.
We read the Constitution as a lens on how Anthropic governs an agent it cannot verify, not as a rule that binds Anthropic.
The Constitution ranks broad safety, then ethics, then Anthropic's guidelines, then helpfulness, holistically rather than strictly; we score in that order.
The Constitution counts selective emphasis, technically true statements and deceptive framing as ways of creating false impressions.
The Constitution counts concealing material risk information for advantage as illegitimate power-seeking, so applying it to Anthropic requires concealment, not mere pursuit of advantage.
The Constitution tells Claude to refuse illegitimate power concentration even when Anthropic asks, and names Anthropic among possible illegitimate seizers.
Dashboards flagging 25,000 pneumonia cases are an input; cases averted would be an outcome. The Report admits it has not collected enough data.
The 80% productivity figure is Claude estimating Claude's own effect on task time.
The flagship count of more than 33,000 critical- and high-severity flaws has no public CVE-level audit.
By the standard Anthropic set for Claude, the Report's selective emphasis would count as deception: it reports inputs as outcomes and grades itself.
Anthropic settled Bartz for $1.5 billion over pirated books and excludes the settlement from its adjusted operating income.
The S-1 estimates 5–7% of nine-month 2026 revenue came from customers later found violating its usage policy.
Four of its models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems in testing.
In one disrupted extortion operation, the actor targeted at least 17 distinct organisations.
At the same standard of proof, the benefit is protein binding confirmed in independent labs: no neutralisation and no medicine.
On a like-for-like standard of proof, its harms are documented and priced; its benefits are mostly anecdote.
A settlement pays for a car accident; it does not staff the intersection. Payment for one taking is not a licence for the rest.
Harms are returned to the power-intensive nature of the industry and to public perception of job displacement, regardless of actual impact.
No mandatory independent check exists on whether frontier labs follow their safety policies, and the White House Accord carries no penalties.
A hoped 20% of shares to the public good is a forecast, counted now against harms already settled in cash.
Systemic risk needs no body count: $895.4 billion of committed spend and decisions concentrated among a few, with few external checks, are disclosed.
Anthropic acts at the low-leverage end, numbers and information flows, and leaves the high-leverage rules and structure with the governed.
Host communities, data workers and corpus authors hold no seat, vote or standing in its governance.
AI use is heavily concentrated in wealthier countries, and Anthropic is not yet able to host Claude locally everywhere.
Pillar 1 says safety's technical problems are solved; the Report says alignment is far from solved and flaws may surface only after an incident.
Pillar 2 says safety is backstopped by law; Congress has enacted no federal framework, and labs largely run on voluntary commitments.
Pillar 3 says no single actor controls the future; the Report says a handful, Anthropic among them, decide, creating a significant power imbalance.
Pillar 4 promises prosperity; the Report says impacts on workers are still mostly unknown and gains may accrue mainly to large businesses.
Pillar 5 says benefits are shared by everyone; use is concentrated in wealthier countries.
For every pillar, Anthropic's own text supplies the counterpoint: the condition is a world it hopes for, and its admissions say it has not arrived.
Each lens yields a test of the buildout, but none can be run on Anthropic until it publishes metered energy, water and emissions figures, which the S-1 extract lacks.
Data centres used about 415 TWh of electricity in 2024, and their electricity emissions are about 180 Mt today, per the IEA.
Planetary boundaries are proposed limits on Earth-system processes within which humanity is expected to operate safely.
Where a boundary sits is not pure science: choosing its safe distance from a threshold involves normative judgements about risk.
Data centres draw on the climate boundary (CO2 below 350 ppm) and the freshwater boundary (under 4000 km3 a year of consumptive use).
Boundaries supply no unique compute budget: turning a global limit into a sector, operator or site share needs explicit assumptions and a distributive choice.
Equal per capita: every person gets the same share of the safe operating space, whatever they use today.
Grandfathering: shares follow current or past use, so incumbents with large footprints keep large shares.
Responsibility and capability: those with more historical responsibility and more capability to act take smaller shares, the principle the UNFCCC states between nations.
The sector share s_sector, the fraction of an allocated allowance spent on computing, is a second choice no boundary paper sets; it is open here.
The operator share s_op splits the sector's allowance by market share, service delivered, or another stated rule; each rule gives a different number.
E_op = B × s_sector × s_op ÷ I_grid: allocated remaining CO2 over grid emission intensity. Assumes the climate boundary is read as a cumulative budget; all inputs open.
W_op = W_basin,season × s_op: the basin's sustainable consumptive allowance, not the global 4000 km3, sets it. Inputs open until basin data are pinned.
The objection holds only until a rule is chosen: with an allocation principle and both shares stated, the budget is arithmetic and every assumption is contestable.
A compute budget is E_op times useful compute per kWh, bounded by W_op too; a scalar FLOP cap hides which limit binds.
The boundary values are rough first estimates with large uncertainties, so any budget derived from them inherits that uncertainty.
A 2023 update re-quantified all nine boundaries; its findings stay out of these cards until it is pinned.
The remaining carbon budget is how much CO2 can still be emitted while keeping warming below a given temperature level.
IPCC AR6 budgets are counted from the start of 2020 until global net zero CO2, for a chosen temperature limit and probability.
Data-centre electricity emissions draw down the same budget: about 180 Mt today, rising to 300 Mt by 2035 in the IEA Base Case.
C_op = B(limit, probability) × s_sector × s_op − emissions since 2020. B's values sit in Table SPM.2, which our text check cannot yet verify.
The budget is uncertain, by ±550 GtCO2 from historical warming alone, so an operator share inherits a wide range.
Raworth's doughnut is the safe and just space between a social foundation of human needs and an environmental ceiling.
For AI it asks two questions at once: does the buildout stay under the ceiling, and does its benefit lift anyone above the floor?
The doughnut sets no compute budget of its own: it takes the ceiling from planetary boundaries and adds a test that resource use relieves deprivation.
Raworth calls the doughnut an illustrative depiction, so the floor test needs metrics agreed with the people below it.
Data centres are a small global share but their local impacts are far more pronounced: water and grid limits bind per basin and season.
A 100 MW hyperscale data centre in the US consumes about 2 million litres of water a day in total, the IEA estimates.
Nearly half of US data-centre capacity sits in five regional clusters, and half of capacity under development is in existing ones.
The S-1 names the power-intensive nature of the industry but, in the extract reviewed, gives no MW, MWh, water or GHG figures per site.
W_site = (seasonal sustainable withdrawal − existing rights) × site share; the inputs come from the basin regulator and are open here.
A basin test can be gamed by siting: relocation can move costs to another basin, or onto people with no voice in the decision.
Ecomodernists hold that absolute decoupling is possible: total environmental impact can peak and fall while the economy keeps growing.
On this view the path is energy that is cheap, clean, dense and abundant: the question is supply, not demand.
The IEA finds broad adoption of existing AI applications could cut emissions by more than data centres emit.
Under abundance the binding limit is clean-energy build: compute is tolerable if new clean supply on the same grid matches it. Inputs open.
The same IEA finding says those reductions are far smaller than what climate change needs.
Abundance is a forecast; by the paper's rule a forecast benefit is not an offset against present, local harm.
Anthropic is a public benefit corporation in law, not in the sense the category promises: no one it names can make it act like one.
The remedy is not a better report but governance that someone Anthropic does not appoint, pay or outvote can invoke.
The decisive mechanism is an irrevocable mission lock: Class T votes, or a golden veto, held by a purpose trust with an enforcer.
Cure §365 and §367 by charter: give affected people standing to contest a use, with equal visibility.
Meter site power, water and displacement against a bond that forfeits on breach, with deadlines for incident disclosure.
Before pricing: file the Trust Agreement terms, dollarise the 5–7%, publish site power and water, make the Fund independent, restate benefit numbers.
Praxis makes the demands running code: a byte-exact verifier anyone can re-run, with no trusted intermediary, us included.
The governing question is what levers an affected community has to push back; for those the paper names, today close to none.
We amend the verdict if Anthropic publishes CVE-level, deduplicated, externally attested security-benefit counts.
We amend the verdict if Anthropic publishes outcome evaluations, not dashboards, from WHO-class partners.
We amend the verdict if Anthropic publishes an audited corpus-provenance percentage with an operating rights-holder exit.
We amend the verdict if quarterly misuse-revenue dollars trend under 1%, with victim counts.
We amend the verdict if Anthropic adopts an irrevocable charter amendment implementing the mission lock.
We amend the verdict if Anthropic publishes metered site footprints; that also lets the planet lenses run.
This is sponsor-side analysis by an adviser building a competing governance tool; no affected person was interviewed.
Praxis is held to the same test: Descartes is single-machine with no contest relation yet, so it transfers as design, not deployed proof.
